newsitem.title: USA: U.S. current account deficit rose in second quarter.
newsitem.headline: U.S. current account deficit rose in second quarter.

text.p: The U.S. current account deficit, the broadest measure of the nation's trade performance, widened during the second quarter because of a bigger shortfall on goods trade, the Commerce Department said Tuesday.

In the three-month period from April through June, the deficit grew to $38.78 billion from $34.87 billion in the first quarter. The second-quarter gap was much wider than the $34.8-billion deficit that Wall Street analysts had forecast.
The department said the overall deficit on goods and services increased to $27.9 billion in the second quarter from $24.2 billion in the first quarter.

The current account is the country's most important trade statistic. It measures trade not only in merchandise and services, but also investment flows between countries as well as grants and aid that the United States supplies to other parts of the world.
Commerce said that transactions involving investment income shifted to a deficit of $1.6 billion in the second quarter from a small surplus of $300 million in the first quarter.

U.S. assets abroad increased by $49.2 billion in the second quarter, slower than the $68.2 billion rise registered in the first three months this year. Foreign assets in the United States grew $80.3 billion, down from a $99.5 billion increase in the first quarter.
Foreign purchases of U.S. Treasury securities nearly tripled to $31.7 billion in the second quarter from $11.8 billion in the first quarter, Commerce said.

Unilateral transfers by the United States fell slightly to $9.3 billion in the second quarter from $10.9 billion in the first quarter, mainly because of a decline in U.S. government grants, the department said.
